title: Just war
hookLine: Augustine and Aquinas set limits on war: just cause, last resort, protect civilians

cards: Crowds have come out to the Jordan River to hear John the Baptist, and he's not gentle with them. Group after group asks the same thing: what shall we do?
Then some soldiers step forward, men who carry swords for a living, under Roman rule. John answers: "Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages."
He doesn't tell them to put down the sword. He doesn't bless whatever they do with it either. He draws lines around it.

teach.b: War is a hard subject in the Bible itself. The prophet Isaiah longed for the day when "they shall beat their swords into plowshares," and "nation shall not lift up sword against nation."
In the garden, when one of his followers drew a sword, Jesus said that "all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword."

And yet nations go to war, and Christians live in those nations, serve in their armies, and lead some of them. So some Christian teachers asked: if war comes, can it ever be right, and under what limits?
Augustine, a bishop in North Africa, wrote to a Roman general about how a soldier could please God.

teach.h: ONLY FOR THE SAKE OF PEACE.
teach.b: War, he answered, may only be waged for the sake of peace, never for its own sake. Elsewhere he named what makes war evil: love of cruelty, and a lust for power.
Much later Thomas Aquinas set conditions: it must be declared by a rightful authority, for a just cause, and with a right intention, aiming at good and away from evil.
Later teachers added that war must be a last resort, and that people who aren't fighting must be protected. Together these became just war teaching. Notice what it is and isn't.
It isn't a cheer for war. It's a fence around it: its rules are reasons not to fight, or limits on how to fight. Not every Christian accepts it; tomorrow, churches that refuse war altogether.
And looking back over this week: open hands, eating with thanks, people not things, mercy with hands, mercy with words, the inner voice, and now limits on war itself.

how: Catholic teaching and some Protestant and Orthodox thinkers use just war criteria to judge when force may be used and how it must be limited, while the historic peace churches reject war altogether; some churches include prayers for those in authority in their services.

games.q: you're a soldier at the Jordan. you've heard John tell the crowds to share their coats and food. you ask him, "and what shall we do?" what does he say?
o: lay down your swords and go home.
do violence to no man, accuse no one falsely, be content with your wages.
games.why: John draws lines around a soldier's work: no violence, no false accusations, no grabbing for more. Christians read his answer in different ways.

practice: Bring to mind a place where people are fighting, or a leader deciding whether they will, and the people far away who will live with that choice.
The first letter to Timothy asks for prayers "for kings, and for all that are in authority": if you pray, you can do that now; if not, simply hold them, and the people under them, in your attention.

wordCard.voice: Just war. Christian teaching that sets limits on war: a just cause, rightful authority, right intention, last resort, and protection for those not fighting.

orig.note: Latin: just war, the name used for this teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: war has limits. Even there, the people who aren't fighting count. Until tomorrow.
